key_terms.meaning: Each function gets its own dedicated LRU box with its own power and wiring, and boxes talk over point-to-point links.
Shared computing modules and a common backplane host many functions as software partitions instead of many separate boxes.
A box on the aircraft that can be swapped on the ramp without opening it or recalibrating the system.
The wiring and connector panel inside a rack that carries power and data between plug-in modules.
A protected slice of processor time and memory so one hosted function cannot corrupt another.
Self-test circuits and software inside an LRU that report faults to the cockpit or to maintenance.
A cockpit where electronic multi-function displays replace most single-function analog dials.
The screen in front of each pilot showing attitude, airspeed, altitude, heading and flight path.
A screen that the crew can switch between navigation map, weather radar, engine and systems pages.
Older name for the attitude and guidance part of the PFD, from the electromechanical ADI.
Older name for the navigation part of the display, showing heading, track, course and map.
Engine indication and crew alerting system: engine parameters plus a ranked list of warning and caution messages.
A display whose symbols are focused at infinity and combined with the outside view by a combiner glass.
A display and sighting system fixed to the pilot's helmet so symbols follow the line of sight.
A one-way, twisted-pair digital bus carrying 32-bit words at 12.5 or 100 kbit/s, one transmitter to many receivers.
A bidirectional military bus at 1 Mbit/s using command/response messages under one bus controller.
An AFDX logical connection from one end system to one or more end systems with a fixed bandwidth and latency guarantee.
The fixed minimum time interval, a power of 2 from 1 ms to 128 ms, between two frames of the same virtual link.
The largest Ethernet frame payload, in bytes, that a virtual link may send in one BAG.
RTCA guidance that sets software assurance objectives according to the failure consequence, from Level A to Level E.
A life cycle where requirements and design are written down one side and verified by matching tests up the other side.
A device that converts a physical quantity such as pressure or position into an electrical signal, or the reverse.
A resistive element glued to a structure; its resistance changes in proportion to the strain it feels.
A circuit that turns a continuous voltage into a number proportional to it, with a stated resolution and reference.
A high-gain differential amplifier used with feedback to amplify, filter or scale sensor signals.

takeaways: The platform drives the avionics: airliners buy safety and schedule regularity, fighters buy mission capability, spacecraft buy autonomy, UAVs buy low size, weight and power.
Federated architecture is simple to certify but heavy; IMA saves weight and space by sharing modules and separating functions with partitions.
The glass cockpit did not remove information, it regrouped it, so the PFD carries control data and the MFD carries navigation and systems data.
HUD and HMD keep symbols in the outside view so the pilot does not lose sight of the runway or the target while reading numbers.
A data bus is a contract: it fixes word format, timing, addressing and error checking so any compliant box can talk to any other.
AFDX turns Ethernet into a deterministic bus by policing each virtual link's BAG and Lmax at the switch.
DO-178B ties the amount of software verification to the consequence of failure, and the V-model makes each requirement traceable to a test.
Transducers and the signal chain in front of the ADC decide measurement accuracy as much as the computer does, so bridge excitation, filtering and resolution all matter.
bank_note: Long answers here usually ask you to compare architectures (federated versus IMA, 429 versus 1553 versus AFDX), to draw and explain display formats, and to link data-bus or software assurance rules to a specific aircraft function.

bank.q: Define avionics system architecture. Compare federated architecture with integrated modular avionics under weight, wiring, certification effort and fault containment.
outline: Definition: the arrangement of computers, sensors, buses and displays and the rules for data flow between them
Federated: one LRU per function, point-to-point wiring, easy to isolate a fault, heavy and many connectors
IMA: shared modules, common backplane, functions run as partitions, saves weight and space
Partitioning by time and memory, with a health monitor and a defined module allocation table
Certification: federated reuses proven boxes; IMA certifies the platform once and then hosts functions
Fault containment and dispatch under minimum equipment list reasoning

bank.q: Explain how the requirements placed on avionics differ for a civil airliner, a military combat aircraft, a spacecraft and a UAV. Give one avionics consequence for each.
outline: Civil: safety, regularity, dispatch reliability, certification to airworthiness rules, navigation and communication fit
Military: mission systems, sensors, survivability, electronic warfare, weapon delivery, high dynamics
Spacecraft: autonomy, telemetry, radiation tolerance, fault recovery without a pilot, low mass and power
UAV: small size, weight and power, remote or autonomous control, datalink dependence, lost-link behaviour
One consequence each: redundant civil buses, MIL-STD-1553 in fighters, watchdog and safe modes in spacecraft, small MEMS sensors in UAVs

bank.q: Describe the standard content of the primary flight display and the multi-function display on a modern airliner, and explain why the information is split that way.
outline: PFD: attitude with pitch ladder and bank scale, airspeed tape, altitude tape, vertical speed, heading, flight path vector, autopilot and flight director modes
PFD: localiser and glide slope scales for approach, radio height
MFD: navigation map with waypoints and weather, engine and fuel pages, system synoptics, checklists
Reason for the split: control information always in the same place for scan; reference and systems information on demand
Colour and shape coding conventions and the use of the attitude as the central reference

bank.q: Explain the ARINC 429 word format and transmission scheme. State the two bit rates and how a receiver knows a word is valid.
outline: One-way simplex transmission, one transmitter to up to many receivers, twisted shielded pair
32-bit word: label, source/destination identifier, data field, sign/status matrix, parity
Odd parity bit and the parity check at the receiver
Bit rates 12.5 kbit/s and 100 kbit/s, self-clocking with a tri-state return-to-zero waveform
Gap between words and how a receiver times out on a silent label
Limitation: no acknowledgement, so redundancy and multiple labels are used for integrity

bank.q: Describe the message formats and operation of MIL-STD-1553B, including the roles of bus controller, remote terminal and bus monitor.
outline: 1 Mbit/s, Manchester II encoded, bidirectional shielded twisted pair, transformer coupled stubs
Word types: command word, data word, status word, each 20 bits with parity
Message types: controller to terminal, terminal to controller, terminal to terminal, mode code
Bus controller owns the schedule; remote terminals reply within a fixed response time; bus monitor listens only
Terminal address field, subaddress, word count, and the status word bits for fault reporting
Why command/response suits military systems: deterministic timing and central fault detection

bank.q: An aircraft is being retrofitted from ARINC 429 to AFDX for a new display system. Using BAG and Lmax, explain how you would size the virtual links and what guarantee the switch gives.
outline: Virtual link defined by source, one or more destinations, a BAG (1 to 128 ms, powers of 2) and a maximum frame size Lmax
Calculate the worst-case bandwidth of a link as Lmax bytes plus protocol overhead divided by BAG
Sum of virtual link bandwidths on a port must stay within the link capacity with a margin
Switch uses a traffic policing and scheduling algorithm so each frame arrives within a bounded latency
Consequence: deterministic delivery for flight-critical data even though the medium is Ethernet
Comparison with the 429 one-way label scheme and the wiring reduction gained

bank.q: A pressure sensor gives a 0 to 50 mV differential output with a 2 kΩ source impedance. Explain the signal chain to produce a clean digital reading in the avionics computer.
outline: Instrumentation amplifier for high input impedance, high common-mode rejection and fixed gain
Bridge or sensor excitation and the effect of excitation drift on the result
Filtering: anti-alias low-pass filter before sampling
ADC resolution and reference; sample rate above twice the highest signal frequency
Quantisation error and the effect of noise on the least significant bit
Conversion to engineering units with calibration coefficients held in non-volatile memory
BITE limits and a validity flag sent with the value

bank.q: Explain how a head-up display produces a collimated image that stays aligned with the runway, and why alignment accuracy is critical.
outline: Symbols generated by a CRT or LCD, magnified and collimated by a lens group so rays leave parallel
Combiner glass reflects the symbols while letting the outside view through
Focus at infinity means the pilot needs no refocusing between symbols and the scene
Alignment to the aircraft reference system through attitude and heading inputs and boresighting
Conformal symbology: flight path vector and runway box drawn where they are in the real world
Error sources: mounting, latency of the attitude data, and the consequence of parallax or misalignment

bank.q: Map a flight-control computer software development onto the V-model for a function whose failure is catastrophic, and list the objectives that this level adds.
outline: Left side: system requirements, high-level software requirements, low-level requirements, design, code
Right side: unit tests against low-level requirements, integration tests against high-level requirements, system tests against system requirements
Bidirectional traceability between every requirement and its test, plus a verification review
Level A adds independence, structural coverage of every statement and decision, and independence between developer and verifier
Configuration index and change control for every artefact
Achieving no unintended function, robustness under abnormal inputs

bank.q: Compare ARINC 429, MIL-STD-1553B and AFDX as backbone buses for a transport aircraft, and justify a choice for flight-critical data against passenger-cabin data.
outline: 429: simplex, low speed, simple and cheap, no acknowledgement, but a wiring explosion with many labels
1553B: 1 Mbit/s, command/response, deterministic, strong fault detection, but military heritage and a single point of schedule control
AFDX: switched full-duplex Ethernet, virtual links with BAG and Lmax, redundancy management, higher bandwidth
Compare bandwidth, determinism, weight, cost, fault detection, certification evidence
Choice: AFDX for flight-critical with duplicated networks, a separate simpler bus for cabin and utility systems
Role of network redundancy and integrity checking in the final argument

bank.q: Evaluate the human-factors advantages and risks of the glass cockpit compared with the analog cockpit, and show how cockpit design compensates for the risks.
outline: Advantages: fewer instruments, integrated data, reconfigurable pages, fewer mechanical failures, automatic alerting
Risks: loss of a display concentrates information, over-reliance, mode confusion, colour and clutter issues, automation complacency
Compensation: display redundancy, reversionary modes, standby attitude airspeed and altitude instruments
Standard layout so the scan pattern is fixed; consistent colour conventions; aural plus visual warnings
Alert ranking and the caution-warning-advisory hierarchy
Design review against human limits: workload, reaction time, legibility, glare, reach

bank.q: An engine indication system must measure turbine temperature, shaft speed, oil pressure and engine vibration. Analyse the transducer choice for each and the signal-conditioning problems involved.
outline: Temperature: thermocouple with cold-junction compensation or a resistive sensor; small signal needs amplification
Speed: magnetic pickup or variable-reluctance sensor giving frequency, or a tachometer generator giving voltage
Pressure: strain gauge or piezoresistive sensor in a bridge, needing excitation and bridge balancing
Vibration: accelerometer, charge or voltage output, wide band, needs anti-alias filtering
Environment: temperature drift, electromagnetic interference, isolation of grounds, sensor excitation stability
Health monitoring: BITE limits, sensor validity and how a failed sensor is declared rather than trusted

bank.q: Assess the fire and electrical interference risks of copper cabling in an aircraft and analyse how fibre-optic links in an AFDX-style network reduce them.
outline: Copper: electromagnetic interference pickup and emission, crosstalk, a short circuit can pass current into a fuel zone, lightning and high-intensity radiated field coupling
Fibre: dielectric, so no current path and no antenna effect, immune to interference, no crosstalk between fibres
Total internal reflection in a core with lower-index cladding carries the light
Single-mode small core for long distance, multimode larger core for shorter runs and cheaper connectors
Costs: connector cleanliness, bend radius, repair complexity, source and detector ageing
Point that fibre removes the interference path but not the need for redundancy and arc or fire protection in the power system

bank.q: A display function is hosted on an IMA module. Evaluate the design choices needed to keep it safe when it shares a module with a lower-criticality function.
outline: Assign a software level from the failure consequence, and note that the higher level dominates the platform
Time and memory partitioning by a certified operating system, with a fixed schedule and protected memory
Budgets: processor time, memory, input-output and bus bandwidth per partition
Health monitoring and partition restart; how an overrun is detected and contained
Data integrity on virtual links between partitions, and the use of a separate network for the display
Evidence for certification: partition analysis, timing analysis, fault injection testing
Evaluate the trade: weight and cost saving against the extra verification of the shared platform

glossary.def: The electronic systems fitted to an aircraft or spacecraft for communication, navigation, display, control and monitoring, and the study of those systems.
The arrangement of computers, sensors, buses and displays in a system and the rules by which they exchange data.
An architecture in which each function has its own dedicated box and its own wiring to the others.
An architecture in which a few shared computing modules and a common network host many software functions as isolated partitions.
An aircraft box that can be removed and replaced as a whole at the aircraft, without internal adjustment.
A plug-in card or unit inside a rack that provides processing, input-output or power conversion.
The fixed wiring and connector assembly at the back of a rack that links the modules plugged into it.
A protected allocation of processor time, memory and input-output that isolates one hosted function from another.
Circuits and software inside a unit that test it, report its health and help isolate a fault.
A cockpit in which electronic multi-function displays replace most separate mechanical instruments.
Primary flight display; the screen presenting attitude, airspeed, altitude, heading and approach guidance.
Multi-function display; a screen that can show navigation, weather, engine and system pages on selection.
Electronic attitude director indicator; the earlier name for the attitude and flight-director part of a PFD.
Electronic horizontal situation indicator; the navigation display showing heading, track, course and map.
Engine indication and crew alerting system; it shows engine parameters and ranked warning and caution messages.
A display that collimates symbols so they appear at infinity and overlays them on the outside view.
Optical processing that makes the rays from an image parallel, so the image appears at infinity.
A display mounted on the pilot's helmet that moves with the head and shows mission or flight symbols.
A simplex digital bus standard using 32-bit words over a twisted pair at 12.5 or 100 kbit/s.
A military command/response serial bus at 1 Mbit/s with a bus controller, remote terminals and a bus monitor.
Avionics full-duplex switched Ethernet; a switched network with guaranteed virtual links for aircraft data.
A defined logical data path in AFDX with a fixed maximum frame size and a fixed minimum frame interval.
The AFDX interface inside an avionics unit that puts data into and takes data out of the switched network.
Bandwidth allocation gap; the shortest permitted interval between frames of one virtual link.
The maximum payload, in bytes, that a virtual link may place in one frame.
An optical fibre with a core small enough to carry one propagation mode, used for long runs.
An optical fibre with a larger core carrying several modes, used for shorter links.
Complete reflection of light at the core-cladding boundary when the ray strikes above the critical angle.
Guidance for airborne software that sets assurance objectives according to the consequence of a software failure.
A development life cycle in which each design stage is verified by a matching test stage on the other arm.
A device that converts one form of energy, such as pressure or movement, into an electrical signal or the reverse.
A resistive foil bonded to a structure whose resistance changes with the strain the structure experiences.
A transducer that produces a signal proportional to acceleration along a defined axis.
Amplifying, filtering, isolating and scaling a sensor signal so a converter can read it accurately.
Analog-to-digital converter; a circuit that converts a voltage into a number with a stated resolution and reference.
Digital-to-analog converter; it converts a number into a voltage or current, often to drive an actuator.
A high-gain differential amplifier that uses external feedback to set gain, offset or filtering.
